I've recently been looking at Lean from the POV of general software engineering. The most I look at it, the more excited I am.

I've written up my thoughts here:

https://paulbutcher.com/lean2.html

I'm still very much a Lean beginner, however, so would welcome any and all feedback.

I think

We can prove (not demonstrate through testing, but mathematically prove), for example, that certain types of XSS vulnerability aren't present.

is too strong a statement. You have proved that some string function does not emit some characters. This is not a proof that there is no XSS. Whether XSS exists is fundamentally browser-dependent and may not even depend on your web-app--old browsers did all kinds of quirky things. If you actually want a proof of there not being XSS, it should probably be in the context of some browser model that takes into account that browser's parsing and rendering. That is what it takes to prove there is no XSS.

you can prove that a function is correct, but proving that things work correctly in the context of a huge piece of software like a browser or kernel is much harder because the models you are working in are much more complex (and the browsers and kernels don't even respect their own internal invariants anyway.) You can of course simplify the model, but then you are really proving it correct in a toy model that makes it IMO closer to a unit test than a mathematical proof.
For the Html stuff it would be cool if you could use some meta-programming to make it look more inline HTML so it's not so boilerplate-y

Hello,

You might be interrested in taking a look at LeanIO, it's inspired by rust Axum library.
It could be used as a backbone for a full server side rendering framework. i like your idea for typesafe routing on frontend links.

And the discussion thread is here

Adam Chlipala of CPDT fame had a very forward-thinking web programming language/compiler/framework called urweb (the reference manual is the highest quality source, but there are papers outlining it as well) that would probably be of interest for those interested in this kind of thing, like "safe by design" strongly typed web programming while figuring out how to deal with the reality of browser and standards complexity.

I think it's still kind of in use in a startup he's running. It was for a brief period of time near the top of the techempower benchmarks as well.

No need to reinvent the wheel, you can take a look at verso. It handles both markdown syntax and html syntax . it even has a component library

You might be interrested in taking a look at LeanIO

Thanks, it looks interesting.

I did, of course, look at Reservoir for any prior art before I dived in and created anything, but LeanIO doesn't seem to be there? Should I be looking somewhere other than Reservoir?

Alfredo Moreira-Rosa said:

No need to reinvent the wheel, you can take a look at verso. It handles both markdown syntax and html syntax . it even has a component library

From the point of view of a generic web app which wants complete control over the DOM it looks like Verso.Output.Html is the relevant bit? This looks interesting, but it seems to be deeply embedded within Verso? Is there some way to get access to just that without pulling in the whole of the rest of Verso?

Reservoir has unfortunately some scanning update issues. Indeed, it's using public github search API that limits the number of results. So reservoir can take many months to finally see a project.
So another way to find if someone did any prior work on a subject is to use the Zulip search feature, but it's not a silver bullet.

For verso, i'm not an expert, you may need to create a dedicated thread to ask this question.

This looks interesting, but it seems to be deeply embedded within Verso? Is there some way to get access to just that without pulling in the whole of the rest of Verso?

FYI, the core Lean library will soon include HTML types very much like those in Verso.
